LGDs will roam farther from sheep in landscapes with less threat of depredating large carnivores, during periods when the moon is more fully illuminated, and during fall.
the distance from a LGD to a human is a function of the LGD's sex and age, time of day, time of year, the moon's phase, and the presence of large, potentially dangerous predators.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
keeping range sheep and LGD groups at least 400 meters from high use recreational areas will likely prevent 9 out of 10 human conflicts with LGDs.

LGDs will roam farther from their sheep when the risk of depredation is lower, and that keeping groups of sheep and their guardian dogs at least 400m from high use recreation sites is likely to prevent 90% or more of agonistic LGDs encounters with humans.
LGDs are effective in preventing livestock predation, and that LGDs do not pose a serious threat to human safety if they are kept at least 400 meters from high use areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LGDs are highly variable in their propensity to wander away from their sheep.

the threat of livestock predation and the risk of LGD human conflicts are both greater in landscapes where gray wolves and griz- zly bears occur than in landscapes where the main predator of livestock is coyotes.
LGD human conflicts can be mitigated with a combination of LGD training and management strategies.
